tool.name: Lua
tool.tagline: Tiny, fast embeddable scripting language for games, editors and config
tool.description: Lua is a small, fast, dynamically typed scripting language designed to be embedded in larger programs. It is the scripting layer of game engines and platforms like Roblox (Luau), LÖVE and World of Warcraft add-ons, of Neovim, Redis, Nginx/OpenResty and many network devices. Its whole design rests on a few powerful ideas (tables, first-class functions, metatables and coroutines), so it is quick to learn and teaches you a lot about how dynamic languages work.

glossary.def: The bigger program that Lua is built into, such as a game engine, the Neovim editor or the Redis database. It runs your Lua scripts and decides which extra functions they get.
A stretch of Lua code that is treated as one unit, such as the body of an if, a loop or a function, ending with end. A whole file is a block too. Local variables live only until their block ends.
In Lua, a table whose numbered keys run 1, 2, 3 ... n with no gaps. Only for sequences does #t reliably give the length.
Describes a function that accepts any number of arguments, written with ... in Lua.
A call that is the very last thing a function does, return f(x). Lua reuses the caller's room on the call stack for it, so tail calls never run out of room.
Lua's obj:method(x) shorthand, which means obj.method(obj, x): it finds the function through the value and passes the value itself as the first argument (self).
In Lua, a short description of text to search for, such as %d+ for "one or more digits". Simpler than regular expressions and written with % instead of a backslash.
In a Lua pattern, a part of the match marked with parentheses, which find, match and gmatch hand back separately.
Lua's for ... in ... loop, which calls an iterator function over and over and stops when it returns nil.
In Lua, a local variable from an outer function that an inner function (a closure) uses. The closure keeps it alive and shares it with other closures made in the same call.
Lua's name for a piece of code that is loaded and run as a unit: a whole file, or a string given to load. A chunk behaves like a function.
Calling a function through pcall or xpcall, so that an error inside it is caught and returned as false plus the error, instead of stopping the script.
A table attached to another table that says what to do in special situations, such as a missing key, + or printing. It is how Lua builds classes and custom operators.
A specially named field in a metatable, like __index or __add, holding what Lua should do when that situation arises.
A Lua value that wraps a block of memory created by C code, such as a file handle or a game object, so Lua scripts can pass it around and use it.
Code that decides which waiting task or coroutine to run next, for example resuming each one when the event it waits for has happened.
A garbage collection method: first mark everything still reachable from the program's variables, then free (sweep away) everything unmarked.
A Lua table whose keys or values don't keep their objects alive: when nothing else refers to such an object, the garbage collector removes the entry.
A function the garbage collector calls once just before freeing an object, set with __gc in Lua, used for last-minute clean-up.
One complete, independent copy of the Lua interpreter created by a C program, with its own variables and memory.
The pile of values through which C code and Lua exchange data: C pushes values on top, reads them by position and pops them off.
A hidden Lua table that only C code can reach, used to keep Lua values alive between calls from C.
When a Lua table outgrows its storage: Lua counts the keys again and moves everything into larger array and hash parts.
A numbered fast slot in a processor, or in Lua's virtual machine, where values being worked on are kept. Lua stores local variables in registers.
Keeping only one copy of each distinct short string, so equal strings share memory and comparing them is instant.

concepts.name: Running Lua
concepts.summary: Run Lua scripts and the interactive prompt, print values and write comments.
concepts.why: Every other lesson assumes you can run a snippet and see what it prints.
concepts.body:
A program is a list of instructions for a computer. Lua is a language for writing them, and a Lua program is usually called a **script**: a plain text file, ending in `.lua`, that is run as it is, with no separate build step. The program that reads and carries out your script is the Lua **interpreter**, a tiny program called `lua`.

Install it with your system's **package manager**, the tool that installs software by name (for example `apt install lua5.4` on Linux or `brew install lua` on macOS). Then open a **terminal**, the text window where you type commands. `lua script.lua` runs a file, and plain `lua` opens a **REPL**: a prompt where you type one line of Lua at a time and see the result straight away.

Words typed after the script name, as in `lua hello.lua a b`, are **command-line arguments**. Your script finds them in a list called `arg`: `arg[1]` is `"a"`.

`print` is a **function**: a named, ready-made piece of code that you run by writing its name followed by parentheses. The values inside the parentheses are its **arguments**. `print` shows them separated by tabs and then ends the line. `io.write` shows them with no separators and no line ending; add `"\n"`, the **newline** character, yourself when you want one.

- A comment, a note for humans that Lua ignores, starts with `--` and runs to the end of the line; `--[[ ... ]]` is a comment that can span several lines.
- Each instruction is a **statement**. Semicolons between statements are optional and rarely used.
- Lua is **case-sensitive**: `print` and `Print` are different names.

Often you won't run Lua yourself. It is built into a bigger **host program**, such as the Neovim editor, the Redis database or a game engine, which runs your scripts and gives them extra functions of its own. The language is the same everywhere, but which ready-made functions exist depends on the host program.

Standalone Lua comes with a **standard library**, groups of functions available without installing anything: `string` (text), `table` (lists), `math`, `io` (reading and writing files), `os` (the operating system: time, environment), `coroutine` and `utf8`.

LuaJIT and Roblox's Luau are popular versions of Lua based on the older Lua 5.1. Most of what you learn here carries over, but a few features added in Lua 5.3 and 5.4 are missing there.
concepts.code:
-- hello.lua: run with `lua hello.lua a b`
print("Hello, Lua!")          --> Hello, Lua!
print(1, "two", true)         --> 1	two	true
io.write("no newline", "\n")  --> no newline
print(_VERSION)               --> Lua 5.4

--[[ A comment
     over several lines ]]
print(#arg)                   --> how many words followed the script name (2 above)
takeaways: `lua file.lua` runs a script; `lua` alone opens a REPL
`--` starts a comment, `--[[ ]]` a multi-line comment
The host program decides which libraries are available
pitfalls: Assuming every host program offers `io` and `os`: host programs that restrict scripts for safety often remove them.

quiz.q: What does print(1, 2) output?
options: An error: print takes one argument
quiz.explain: print accepts any number of arguments and separates them with tabs.

quiz.q: Your script runs inside a game engine instead of the standalone lua program. What may be different?
options: Which ready-made functions and libraries are available
quiz.explain: The language is the same everywhere; the host program decides which libraries and extra functions your script can use.

concepts.name: Values, types and variables
concepts.summary: Store values in variables, know Lua's eight types and its two kinds of number, and always declare variables local.
concepts.why: Knowing the types and the local/global rule prevents the most common Lua bugs.
concepts.body:
A program works with **values**: numbers like `42`, text like `"hi"`, `true` and `false`. A **variable** is a name that holds a value: `local age = 30` creates a variable named `age` holding 30; `age = 31` later replaces the value.

Every value has a **type**, its kind, and `type(v)` gives the type's name as text. Lua is **dynamically typed**: the value carries the type, not the variable, so one variable can hold a number now and text later. There are eight types:

- `nil`: "no value". A variable that was never given a value holds `nil`.
- `boolean`: `true` or `false` (a **boolean**).
- `number`: any number.
- `string`: a piece of text (a **string**).
- `table`: Lua's way of grouping values (the Tables lesson).
- `function`: code you can run (the Functions lesson).
- `thread` and `userdata`: advanced types, covered much later.

Since Lua 5.3 a number is either an **integer**, a whole number such as `3`, or a **floating-point number** ("float"), a number with a decimal point such as `3.0` or `2.5`; `math.type(x)` tells them apart. `/` always gives a float (`7 / 2` is `3.5`). `//` is **floor division**, which rounds down to a whole number (`7 // 2` is `3`). `%` gives the remainder, and `^` raises to a power (`2 ^ 10` is `1024.0`, always a float).

Integers have a largest value, `math.maxinteger`; going past it wraps round to the most negative integer, silently.

Write strings with single quotes, double quotes, or `[[ ... ]]` for text spanning several lines. Join them with `..`, which is called **concatenation**: `"Lua" .. "!"`. `#s` gives the length in **bytes**, the units text is stored in (one per plain English letter). Strings are **immutable**: you never change one, you build a new one.

Variables are global by default: assigning to a name you never declared creates a **global variable**, visible to the whole program, and reading a misspelled name quietly gives `nil` instead of an error. Always declare with `local`. A **local variable** exists only inside the **block** where you created it, the stretch of code that ends with the matching `end` (or the whole file), so it can't clash with other code, and it's faster.

Several variables can be set at once: `local a, b = 1, 2`, and `a, b = b, a` swaps them. Extra values are thrown away and missing ones become `nil`.
concepts.code:
local n, f = 10, 10.0
print(type(n), math.type(n), math.type(f))  --> number	integer	float
print(n == f)          --> true (same number)
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2)   --> 3.5	3
print(2 ^ 10)          --> 1024.0
print(math.maxinteger + 1 == math.mininteger) --> true (wraps round)

local s = "Lua" .. " " .. 5.4
print(s, #s)           --> Lua 5.4	7

local a, b, c = 1, 2
print(a, b, c)         --> 1	2	nil
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)            --> 2	1

do                     -- do ... end marks a block
  local inside = 1     -- exists only until the matching end
  counter = 1          -- oops: no local, so this creates a global
end
print(inside, counter) --> nil	1
takeaways: Eight types; `type(v)` returns the name as a string
Numbers are integers or floats; `/` gives a float, `//` rounds down
Declare everything `local`; undeclared names are globals
pitfalls: A typo in a variable name silently reads `nil` instead of raising an error.

quiz.q: What does 7 // 2 evaluate to in Lua 5.4?
quiz.explain: // is floor division; with two integers it returns the integer 3.

quiz.q: What happens when you write `x = 5` without `local`?
options: x exists only until the next end
x exists only in this file
quiz.explain: Undeclared variables are globals in Lua, which is why local should be the default.

concepts.name: Conditions and loops
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if/elseif and repeat work with while, repeat-until and the counting for loop, plus Lua's rule for what counts as true.
concepts.why: Deciding and repeating are how every program works, and Lua's rule for what counts as true differs from many languages.
concepts.body:
A program decides what to do with a **conditional**: `if cond then ... elseif other then ... else ... end`. The code after `then` runs only when its condition is true. Every block in Lua is closed with `end`.

What counts as true? Lua's rule is simple: only `nil` and `false` count as false; they are **falsy**, and every other value is **truthy**. Zero and the empty string are truthy, which surprises people coming from Python, JavaScript or C.

Comparisons use `==` (equal), `~=` (not equal), `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Values of different types are never equal, so `1 == "1"` is false.

The words `and`, `or` and `not` are **operators**: signs or words that combine values. `and` and `or` stop as soon as the answer is known, which is called **short-circuit evaluation**, and give back one of their two values rather than a plain true or false: `nil or "guest"` is `"guest"`. Two idioms follow. `x = x or 10` gives `x` a **default value** when it is nil. `cond and a or b` picks `a` or `b` like a one-line if, but it breaks when `a` is `false` or `nil`.

A **loop** repeats a block, and each pass through it is one **iteration**:

- `while cond do ... end` checks the condition before each pass.
- `repeat ... until cond` runs at least once and stops when the condition becomes true; locals created inside can be used in the `until` condition.
- `for i = start, stop, step do ... end` counts: `i` starts at `start` and changes by `step` (1 if you leave it out) until it passes `stop`. `i` is local to the loop.

`break` leaves the innermost loop. Lua has no `continue`; instead, put a label `::continue::` just before the loop's `end` and jump to it with `goto continue`, or wrap the rest of the loop body in an `if`.
concepts.code:
local n = -3
if n < 0 then print("negative")
elseif n == 0 then print("zero")
else print("positive") end         --> negative

if 0 then print("0 is true") end   --> 0 is true
local name = nil
print(name or "anonymous")         --> anonymous

for i = 10, 1, -3 do io.write(i, " ") end  --> 10 7 4 1
print()

local i = 0
repeat i = i + 1 until i * i > 20
print(i)                           --> 5

for k = 1, 5 do
  if k % 2 == 0 then goto continue end   -- skip even numbers
  io.write(k, " ")                 --> 1 3 5
  ::continue::
end
print()
takeaways: Only `nil` and `false` are falsy; 0 and "" are true
`x or default` is the default-value idiom
Not-equal is `~=`; there is no `continue`, use `goto continue`
pitfalls: Writing `cond and a or b` when `a` can be false or nil: you always get `b`.

quiz.q: Which values are falsy in Lua?
quiz.explain: Lua treats every value except nil and false as true, including 0 and the empty string.

quiz.q: What does `local who = nil or "guest"` store in who?
quiz.explain: or gives back its second value when the first is falsy, so who becomes "guest".

concepts.name: Tables: arrays and dictionaries
concepts.summary: The table is Lua's only data structure: use it as a numbered list or as a dictionary of named fields.
concepts.why: Everything beyond the simplest script is built from tables, so you need them from day one.
concepts.body:
Programs often need many values together: a shopping list, a person's name and age, every player's score. A **data structure** is a way of organising such values, and Lua has exactly one: the **table**.

A table stores **key-value pairs**: each value is filed under a key, like words and their meanings in a dictionary. Any value except `nil` can be a key. That one idea covers two common shapes: an **array**, a numbered list (keys 1, 2, 3...), and a **dictionary**, where you look values up by name (keys like `"name"` and `"age"`).

Build a table with braces. Values listed without keys get the keys 1, 2, 3...: in `{"a", "b"}`, `t[1]` is `"a"`. Lua counts from **1**, not 0 as most languages do. That position number is the **index**.

`{x = 1}` stores 1 under the text key `"x"`; such a named entry is a **field**, and `t.x` is shorthand for `t["x"]`. For any other key, use brackets: `{[10] = "ten", ["my key"] = true}`.

Reading a missing key gives `nil`. Assigning `nil` to a key deletes it.

`#t` gives the length of the numbered part, but it's only reliable for a **sequence**: keys 1 to n with no `nil` gaps. To add at the end, write `t[#t + 1] = v` or call `table.insert(t, v)`. `table.remove(t)` takes the last item off, `table.concat(t, ", ")` joins strings into one, and `table.sort(t)` sorts the table in place.

Assigning a table to another variable doesn't copy it: both names now lead to the same table, because the variable holds a **reference** to it. Two tables are `==` only if they are the very same table. That makes tables cheap to pass around, but you must copy one yourself when you want an independent version.

Later lessons show tables standing in for objects, modules and more.
concepts.code:
local fruits = {"apple", "banana"}
fruits[#fruits + 1] = "cherry"
table.insert(fruits, 1, "kiwi")        -- insert at position 1
print(#fruits, fruits[1])              --> 4	kiwi
print(table.concat(fruits, ", "))      --> kiwi, apple, banana, cherry

local point = {x = 3, y = 4, ["z-axis"] = 0}
point.x = nil                          -- delete a key
print(point.x, point["z-axis"])        --> nil	0

local alias = fruits
alias[1] = "lime"
print(fruits[1])                       --> lime (same table)
print({} == {})                        --> false

table.sort(fruits)
print(table.concat(fruits, " "))       --> apple banana cherry lime
print(table.remove(fruits), #fruits)   --> lime	3
takeaways: Tables are Lua's only data structure: lists, dictionaries and more
Lists start at index 1; `t.x` means `t["x"]`
`#t` is reliable only for sequences without nil gaps
Assigning a table shares it; `==` checks for the very same table
pitfalls: Storing nil in the middle of a list, which makes `#t` and loops over the list unreliable.

quiz.q: After t = {10, 20, 30}, what is t[0]?
quiz.explain: Listed values start at index 1, so key 0 was never set and reading it returns nil.

quiz.q: What does local b = a do when a is a table?
options: Makes b lead to the same table
quiz.explain: A variable holds a reference to a table, so both names now point to the same table.

concepts.name: Functions and multiple returns
concepts.summary: Write your own functions, return several values, accept any number of arguments and pass functions around.
concepts.why: Functions are values in Lua, just like numbers and tables, and they are the main tool for structuring code.
concepts.body:
You've been calling ready-made functions like `print`. Now write your own: `local function add(a, b) return a + b end`. `a` and `b` are **parameters**, names for the inputs; `return` hands back the **return value**. Call it as `add(2, 3)`. Always write `local function`: without `local`, the function becomes a global.

In Lua, functions are values, like numbers and strings. You can store them in variables and tables, pass them to other functions as arguments, and return them from functions.

Arguments are matched to parameters by position. Missing ones are `nil` and extra ones are ignored, so `a = a or 1` is the usual way to give a parameter a default value.

A function can **return several values**: `return q, r`. The caller takes as many as it asks for: `local q, r = divmod(17, 5)`. One rule matters: a call hands over all its values only when it is the last **expression** (a piece of code that produces a value) in a list. Anywhere else, or wrapped in extra parentheses, it is cut to its first value.

A function that accepts any number of arguments is a **variadic function**; write `...` as its last parameter. Inside, `select("#", ...)` counts the arguments (including `nil`s) and `{...}` collects them into a table. `table.unpack(t)` does the reverse, spreading a table out into separate arguments.

When the only argument is a table or a string in quotes, you can leave out the parentheses: `f{x = 1}` and `print "hi"`. Passing one table is the usual way to fake named arguments: `greet{name = "Ana"}`.

A function may call itself, which is **recursion**. Each unfinished call normally takes room on the **call stack**, Lua's list of which function called which, so very deep recursion fails with an error once that room runs out. But when a function ends with `return f(x)`, a **tail call**, Lua reuses the current call's room, so such calls can go on as long as you like.
concepts.code:
local function divmod(a, b)
  return a // b, a % b
end
local q, r = divmod(17, 5)
print(q, r)                    --> 3	2
print(divmod(17, 5), "end")    --> 3	end (cut to one value)
print((divmod(17, 5)))         --> 3

local function sum(...)        -- variadic: any number of arguments
  local args = {...}
  local total = 0
  for i = 1, #args do total = total + args[i] end
  return total, select("#", ...)
end
print(sum(1, 2, 3))            --> 6	3
print(sum(table.unpack({4, 5}))) --> 9	2

local function greet(opts)     -- one table as "named arguments"
  local name = opts.name or "world"
  return "hello " .. name
end
print(greet{name = "Ana"})     --> hello Ana
takeaways: Use `local function` so functions don't become globals
A call gives all its results only as the last item in a list
`...`, `select("#", ...)` and `table.unpack` handle any number of arguments
`f{...}` with a table fakes named arguments
pitfalls: Expecting `f(), x` to keep all of f's return values; only a call in the last position does.

quiz.q: local function two() return 1, 2 end. What does print(two(), 9) print?
quiz.explain: two() isn't the last expression, so it is cut to its first result.

concepts.name: Strings and patterns
concepts.summary: Format, search and change text with the string library and Lua patterns.
concepts.why: Working with text is a daily task, and Lua patterns look like regular expressions but behave differently.
concepts.body:
All string functions live in the `string` table, and Lua links every string to that table, so `s:upper()` is the same as `string.upper(s)`. This **colon syntax**, `value:name(...)`, calls a function found through the value and passes the value itself as the first argument; a function called this way is often called a **method**.

Indexes start at 1, and negative indexes count from the end: `s:sub(-3)` is the last three bytes. `string.format` fills values into a template using placeholders, as C's `printf` does: `%d` a whole number, `%5.2f` a decimal with 2 digits after the point in 5 characters, `%s` text, `%q` text in quotes that Lua could read back. `s:rep(n)`, `s:reverse()` and `s:byte()`/`string.char` round out the basics.

A **pattern** is a short description of the text you're looking for. Lua patterns are a lightweight alternative to **regular expressions**, the pattern language most other tools use. Character classes are written with `%`: `%d` a digit, `%a` a letter, `%s` a space, `%w` a letter or digit; the uppercase version means "anything but". Repeat markers follow a piece: `*` (0 or more), `+` (1 or more), `?` (optional) and `-` (0 or more, but as few as possible). Parentheses mark a **capture**, a part of the match to hand back separately. There is no "this or that" (`|`) and no `{n,m}` counts.

- `s:find(p)` returns the start and end index, plus captures.
- `s:match(p)` returns the captures (or the whole match).
- `s:gmatch(p)` gives every match in turn, for use in a `for` loop (see Iterators).
- `s:gsub(p, repl)` replaces; `repl` can be a string with `%1`, a table or a function.

Because `%` escapes magic characters, write `%.` for a literal dot. Pass `true` as the fourth argument of `find` to search for a plain **substring**, an exact piece of text, with no pattern rules.

Strings are bytes. Letters beyond plain English, like é, are usually stored as **UTF-8**, which uses several bytes for them; use the `utf8` library (`utf8.len`, `utf8.codes`) to count or walk through real characters.
concepts.code:
local s = "Lua 5.4 was released in 2020"
print(s:upper():sub(1, 3))           --> LUA
print(s:find("%d+"))                 --> 5	5
print(s:match("(%d+)%.(%d+)"))       --> 5	4

for word in s:gmatch("%a+") do io.write(word, ",") end
print()                              --> Lua,was,released,in,

local out, n = s:gsub("%d+", function(d) return "<" .. d .. ">" end)
print(out, n)  --> Lua <5>.<4> was released in <2020>	3

print(("key = value"):match("^(%w+)%s*=%s*(%w+)$"))  --> key	value
print(string.format("%-5s|%6.2f|%q", "ab", math.pi, "hi")) --> ab   |  3.14|"hi"
print(#"héllo", utf8.len("héllo"))   --> 6	5
takeaways: `s:method()` calls `string.method(s)`
Patterns use `%` classes (`%d`, `%a`, `%s`) and have no `|` for "this or that"
`gsub` accepts a string, table or function as the replacement
Use `utf8` functions for character counts in UTF-8 text
pitfalls: Using `.` or `-` unescaped when you mean the literal character; write `%.` and `%-`.

quiz.q: What does ("a.b.c"):gsub(".", "-") return as its first value?
quiz.explain: An unescaped . matches any character, so all five characters are replaced; use %. for a literal dot.

concepts.name: Iterators: pairs, ipairs and generic for
concepts.summary: Loop over tables with pairs and ipairs, and write your own iterators.
concepts.why: The generic for is how you go through every table, file and list of matches in Lua.
concepts.body:
An **iterator** is a function that hands out the next item each time it is called and `nil` when there are no more. The **generic for** loop, `for k, v in iterator do ... end`, calls it over and over until it returns `nil`.

- `ipairs(t)` walks `t[1]`, `t[2]`, ... in order and stops at the first `nil`. Use it for lists.
- `pairs(t)` visits every key in the table, in **no particular order**. Use it for dictionaries, and never rely on the order. To go through keys in a fixed order, collect the keys, `table.sort` them, then loop.

You must not add new keys to a table while traversing it with `pairs` (assigning to existing fields, including setting them to `nil`, is allowed).

Writing your own iterator is easy: return a function that remembers where it is (a closure, see Closures) and produces the next value on each call. Under the hood the generic for also accepts two extra values, a fixed state and the previous position, which it passes to the iterator each time; that's how `pairs` and `ipairs` avoid creating a new function for every loop. Lua 5.4 adds a fourth value, used to clean up automatically when the loop ends.

Iterators let you handle data one piece at a time: `io.lines(path)` returns an iterator over a file's lines and `s:gmatch` one over pattern matches, so you can work through large inputs without first building a table that holds them all.
concepts.code:
local scores = {ana = 90, bo = 72, cy = 85}

local names = {}
for name in pairs(scores) do names[#names + 1] = name end
table.sort(names)                      -- fixed order
for i, name in ipairs(names) do
  print(i, name, scores[name])
end
--> 1	ana	90
--> 2	bo	72
--> 3	cy	85

local function range(n, step)
  local i = 0
  return function()                    -- closure iterator
    i = i + (step or 1)
    if i <= n then return i end
  end
end
for x in range(10, 4) do io.write(x, " ") end  --> 4 8
print()

for i, v in ipairs({1, 2, nil, 4}) do io.write(v, " ") end --> 1 2
print()
takeaways: `ipairs` for arrays (stops at the first nil), `pairs` for all keys
`pairs` order is unspecified; sort keys when order matters
An iterator is just a function that returns nil when finished
pitfalls: Adding keys to a table while going through it with pairs: Lua doesn't allow it, and the loop may skip or repeat keys.

quiz.q: for i, v in ipairs({1, 2, nil, 4}) prints how many elements?
quiz.explain: ipairs stops at the first nil, so only 1 and 2 are visited.

concepts.name: Closures and upvalues
concepts.summary: Functions remember the local variables around them, giving you private state without needing objects.
concepts.why: Closures power callbacks, iterators, result caching and simple objects throughout Lua code.
concepts.body:
A variable's **scope** is the part of the code where its name can be used. Lua's scope is lexical, decided by where code is written: a function can read and write the local variables of the blocks around it, even after those blocks have finished running. A function that does this is a **closure**, and each outside local it uses is called an **upvalue**.

Each time Lua reaches a `function ... end` expression, it creates a new closure linked to the current copies of those outside variables. Two closures created in the same call share the same upvalue, so they see each other's updates.

This gives you private state cheaply. A function that makes counters returns a function that adds one to a local; nobody outside can touch the count. **Memoization**, remembering results so a slow calculation runs only once per input, is a closure over a **cache** table, a table of saved results. A **callback**, a function you hand to other code to be called later (say, when a key is pressed), carries along the variables it needs.

Loops create a fresh local for each iteration: closures created inside `for i = 1, 3` each keep their own `i`.

Scope rules worth remembering:

- A `local` is visible from the statement after its declaration to the end of its block.
- `local function f` makes `f` visible inside its own body, so it can call itself; `local f = function` does not.
- `do ... end` creates a block purely to limit scope.

Accessing upvalues is slightly slower than locals but much faster than globals, which is why performance-sensitive code often caches globals in locals (`local insert = table.insert`).
concepts.code:
local function counter()
  local n = 0
  return function() n = n + 1; return n end,
         function() return n end
end
local inc, get = counter()
inc(); inc()
print(get())                 --> 2 (shared upvalue)

local fns = {}
for i = 1, 3 do fns[i] = function() return i end end
print(fns[1](), fns[3]())    --> 1	3 (fresh i per iteration)

local function memoize(f)
  local cache = {}
  return function(x)
    local v = cache[x]
    if v == nil then v = f(x); cache[x] = v end
    return v
  end
end
local slow_sq = memoize(function(x) print("computing", x); return x * x end)
print(slow_sq(4))            --> computing	4 / 16
print(slow_sq(4))            --> 16 (cached)
takeaways: A closure uses the surrounding locals (upvalues) themselves, not copies
Closures created in one call share the same upvalues
Each loop iteration gets a fresh loop variable
pitfalls: Using `local f = function() ... f() ... end` for recursion: inside the body `f` still means the global `f`, which is nil.

quiz.q: Two closures returned from the same call to counter() both use n. What happens when one increments it?
options: The other sees the new value
Only the first call is affected
quiz.explain: Closures created in the same call share the upvalue, so a change made through one is seen by the other.

concepts.name: Modules and require
concepts.summary: Split code into files that return a table, and load them with require.
concepts.why: Every real Lua project and every host program (Neovim, LÖVE) organises code as modules.
concepts.body:
A **module** is a file of related code that other files can load and use. In Lua it is just a file that returns a value, almost always a table of functions. Keep everything else `local` and make available only what you put in that table.

`require("mylib.util")` turns the dots into **directory** (folder) separators and tries each pattern in `package.path` (for Lua files, e.g. `./?.lua;./?/init.lua;...`, where `?` is replaced by the name) and `package.cpath` (for libraries written in C). The loaded result is saved in `package.loaded`, a **cache**, so the file runs **once** no matter how many times it is required, and every caller shares the same table.

Conventions:

- Return a table; don't set globals from a module.
- Name the local table `M` (or the module name) and `return M` at the end.
- `require` passes the module name as `...` to the file's code (Lua calls a file or string of code a **chunk**), useful for loading neighbouring modules.

To reload during development set `package.loaded[name] = nil` and require again. Host programs usually add their own search paths: Neovim looks in the `lua/` folder of each plugin, and LuaRocks, Lua's package manager, installs libraries into folders that it adds to the paths.

At a lower level, `load(str)` turns a string of Lua code into a function you can call, and `dofile`/`loadfile` do the same for files, without the cache.
concepts.code:
-- Simulate a file mathx.lua via package.preload
package.preload["mathx"] = function(name)
  local M = {}
  local function check(n) assert(type(n) == "number", "number expected") end
  function M.clamp(x, lo, hi)
    check(x)
    return math.max(lo, math.min(hi, x))
  end
  print("loading " .. name)
  return M
end

local mx = require("mathx")      --> loading mathx
local again = require("mathx")   -- cached: prints nothing
print(mx == again)               --> true
print(mx.clamp(15, 0, 10))       --> 10
print(mx.check)                  --> nil (private)
print(package.path ~= nil)       --> true

local f = load("return 2 + 3")
print(f())                       --> 5
takeaways: A module is a file that returns a table
`require` runs a module once and caches it in `package.loaded`
Keep helpers `local`; export only through the returned table
pitfalls: Setting globals from a module, which leaks names into every other module.

quiz.q: A module file is required from three different files. How many times does its top-level code run?
quiz.explain: require caches the result in package.loaded and returns the cached value afterwards.

concepts.name: Errors, pcall and assert
concepts.summary: Raise errors with error and assert, and catch them with pcall and xpcall.
concepts.why: Lua has no try/catch blocks like other languages; knowing pcall is essential for scripts and plugins that don't fall over.
concepts.body:
`error(msg)` raises an error: it stops the current function and every function that called it, until something catches the error (or the script ends with the message). The message can be any value, including a table carrying details. With a string, Lua adds the position in front (`file:line:`); pass a level as the second argument to point at the caller instead (`error(msg, 2)`), or `0` to add nothing.

`assert(v, msg)` is an **assertion**, a check that something you expect is true: it raises `msg` when `v` is falsy and otherwise returns all its arguments, so `local f = assert(io.open(path))` is idiomatic: `io.open` returns `nil, message` on failure and `assert` turns that into an error.

To catch errors, call the function through `pcall`, a **protected call**: `local ok, result = pcall(f, arg1, arg2)`. On success `ok` is `true` followed by f's results; on failure `ok` is `false` and the second value is the error object. `xpcall(f, handler, ...)` also calls your handler function at the moment of the error, before the calls in progress are abandoned, which is where you grab `debug.traceback()`: a **stack trace** listing which function called which.

Two error styles coexist in Lua code:

- Return `nil, errmsg` for expected failures (file not found, bad input). The standard library does this.
- Raise with `error` for bugs and unrecoverable situations.

For clean-up, Lua 5.4 adds to-be-closed variables: `local f <close> = obj` calls the value's `__close` function (see Metatables) when the block ends, normally or by an error.
concepts.code:
local function parse_age(s)
  local n = tonumber(s)
  if not n then error({code = "EINVAL", input = s}) end
  if n < 0 then error("age must be >= 0", 2) end
  return n
end

local ok, err = pcall(parse_age, "abc")
print(ok, type(err), err.code)         --> false	table	EINVAL

ok, err = pcall(parse_age, "42")
print(ok, err)                         --> true	42

local f, msg = io.open("/no/such/file")
print(f, msg ~= nil)                   --> nil	true

ok, err = xpcall(function() local t = nil; return t.x end,
                 function(e) return "handled: " .. e end)
print(ok, err:match("attempt to index") ~= nil)  --> false	true
takeaways: `pcall(f, ...)` returns `true, results` or `false, err`
`assert(v, msg)` passes values through or raises
Expected failures return `nil, msg`; bugs raise with `error`
pitfalls: Calling `pcall(f(x))`: that calls f outside the protection; write `pcall(f, x)`.

quiz.q: Which call protects f against errors when passing it the argument x?
quiz.explain: pcall must call f itself; f(x) would run before pcall gets control.

concepts.name: Metatables and metamethods
concepts.summary: Customise how tables behave for indexing, arithmetic, comparison, calling and printing.
concepts.why: Metatables are the mechanism behind classes, default values, read-only tables and custom operators in Lua.
concepts.body:
Every table can have a **metatable**: an ordinary table whose specially named fields, the **metamethods**, define what happens when the table meets an operation it can't handle by itself, such as `+` or a missing key. Set it with `setmetatable(t, mt)` (which returns `t`) and read it with `getmetatable(t)`.

The most important ones:

- `__index` runs when a key is **missing**. If it is a table, Lua looks the key up there (and in that table's `__index`, and so on); if it is a function it is called with `(t, key)`. This is how default values and inheritance (one table borrowing another's functions, see the next lesson) work.
- `__newindex` runs when assigning to a missing key; use `rawset` inside it to actually store.
- `__add`, `__sub`, `__mul`, `__eq`, `__lt`, `__le`, `__concat`, `__unm`, `__len` give operators like `+`, `==` and `#` a meaning for your tables, which is called **overloading**.
- `__call` makes a table callable; `__tostring` controls `tostring` and `print`; `__close` and `__gc` handle clean-up.

`rawget`, `rawset`, `rawequal` and `rawlen` skip the metamethods, which you need inside a metamethod so it doesn't trigger itself again and again.

Strings share one metatable whose `__index` is the `string` table, which is why `s:upper()` works. Only tables (and **userdata**, blocks of data made by C code) can have their own individual metatables set from Lua.

Lua looks metamethods up directly in the metatable when the operation happens, so they must be there by then; the one exception to watch is `__gc`, which must already be in the table when you call `setmetatable`.
concepts.code:
local Vec = {}
Vec.__index = Vec
local function vec(x, y) return setmetatable({x = x, y = y}, Vec) end

Vec.__add = function(a, b) return vec(a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y) end
Vec.__eq = function(a, b) return a.x == b.x and a.y == b.y end
Vec.__tostring = function(v) return "(" .. v.x .. ", " .. v.y .. ")" end
function Vec.len(v) return math.sqrt(v.x ^ 2 + v.y ^ 2) end

local a = vec(3, 4)
print(tostring(a + vec(1, 1)))   --> (4, 5)
print(a == vec(3, 4))            --> true
print(a:len())                   --> 5.0 (found through __index)

local defaults = setmetatable({}, {__index = function(t, k) return 0 end})
defaults.hits = defaults.hits + 1
print(defaults.hits, defaults.misses)   --> 1	0

local readonly = setmetatable({}, {__newindex = function() error("read-only", 2) end})
print(pcall(function() readonly.x = 1 end))  --> false	...read-only
takeaways: `__index` handles missing keys: a table to delegate, a function to compute
Arithmetic, comparison, call and tostring are all overridable
Use `rawget`/`rawset` inside metamethods to avoid recursion
pitfalls: Expecting `__index` to run for keys that exist: it only fires on missing keys.

quiz.q: When does a table's __index metamethod run?
options: When reading a key that is absent from the table
Only when calling a method with :
quiz.explain: __index is a fallback for lookups that find nil in the table itself.

quiz.q: Why use rawset inside __newindex?
options: It is required for numeric keys
quiz.explain: The key is still missing, so a normal assignment would recurse into __newindex forever.

concepts.name: Classes and inheritance with metatables
concepts.summary: Build classes, methods and single inheritance from tables, __index and the colon syntax.
concepts.why: Most Lua code (games, plugins, libraries) uses this pattern for objects.
concepts.body:
Many languages organise code as **objects**, bundles of data plus the functions (methods) that work on it, made from a **class**, a blueprint shared by many objects. Lua has no class keyword. Instead a class is a table of methods, and each **instance**, one object made from the class, is a table whose metatable has `__index` pointing at the class. Missing fields, the methods, are then found on the class.

The **colon syntax** wires up `self`. `function Account:deposit(v)` defines a function with a hidden first parameter `self`, and `acc:deposit(10)` calls `Account.deposit(acc, 10)`. Mixing `.` and `:` is the classic bug: `acc.deposit(10)` passes 10 as `self`.

A typical **constructor**, the function that makes new objects, is `function Class.new(...)`: it creates a table, sets the metatable and gives the fields their starting values. Setting `Class.__index = Class` lets the class serve as its own metatable.

**Inheritance**, building a class on top of another, chains these lookups: give the **subclass** a metatable whose `__index` is the parent, or **base class** (`setmetatable(Sub, {__index = Base})`). A missing method is searched in the instance, then the subclass, then the base. Call the parent's method explicitly with `Base.method(self, ...)`; there is no `super`.

Privacy is a convention (an underscore prefix) unless you use closures instead of tables for state. Many projects use a small class library (middleclass, classic), but those are thin layers over exactly this mechanism, so it pays to understand it directly.
concepts.code:
local Account = {}
Account.__index = Account

function Account.new(owner, balance)
  return setmetatable({owner = owner, balance = balance or 0}, Account)
end
function Account:deposit(v) self.balance = self.balance + v end
function Account:describe() return self.owner .. ": " .. self.balance end

local Savings = setmetatable({}, {__index = Account})
Savings.__index = Savings
function Savings.new(owner, balance, rate)
  local self = Account.new(owner, balance)
  self.rate = rate
  return setmetatable(self, Savings)
end
function Savings:add_interest() self:deposit(self.balance * self.rate) end
function Savings:describe()
  return Account.describe(self) .. " @" .. self.rate   -- call "super"
end

local s = Savings.new("ana", 100, 0.05)
s:add_interest()
print(s:describe())                --> ana: 105.0 @0.05
print(getmetatable(s) == Savings)  --> true
takeaways: A class is a method table used as the instances' `__index`
`obj:m(x)` is `obj.m(obj, x)`; define methods with `:` to get `self`
Inheritance = the subclass table's own `__index` points at the base
pitfalls: Calling a method with a dot (`obj.m()`), so `self` is missing or wrong.

quiz.q: What is obj:greet("hi") shorthand for?
quiz.explain: The colon call passes the receiver as the first argument, which becomes self.

concepts.name: Coroutines
concepts.summary: Pause and resume functions with coroutine.yield and resume to write generators and tasks that take turns.
concepts.why: Coroutines drive game scripting, waiting for network or file replies in OpenResty and Neovim, and elegant generators.
concepts.body:
A **coroutine** is a function that can pause itself in the middle and be resumed later, carrying on exactly where it stopped, with its own call stack. Coroutines take turns politely: only one runs at a time, and it keeps running until it explicitly pauses (yields).

- `coroutine.create(f)` makes a coroutine (type `thread`) without running it.
- `coroutine.resume(co, ...)` starts or continues it. It returns `true` plus the values passed to `yield` (or returned at the end), or `false, err` if the coroutine raised an error.
- `coroutine.yield(...)` suspends the current coroutine; the values become resume's results, and the arguments of the next `resume` become yield's return values.
- `coroutine.status(co)` is `suspended`, `running`, `normal` or `dead`.
- `coroutine.wrap(f)` returns a function that resumes on each call and re-raises errors, perfect for **generators**, functions that produce a series of values one at a time, used in a generic for.

Because the stack is preserved, a coroutine can yield from deep inside nested calls. That lets you write code that reads top to bottom (wait for an animation, then for input, then for a timer) while a **scheduler**, the code that decides which paused coroutine to resume next, wakes it up when each event happens. OpenResty and many Neovim plugins turn callback-based functions into straight-line code exactly this way.

`coroutine.close(co)` (5.4) ends a paused coroutine for good and runs its pending clean-up. A coroutine can't pause while inside a function written in C unless that C function was written to allow it.
concepts.code:
local function numbers(limit)
  return coroutine.wrap(function()
    for i = 1, limit do coroutine.yield(i, i * i) end
  end)
end
for n, sq in numbers(3) do io.write(n, ":", sq, " ") end
print()                               --> 1:1 2:4 3:9

local co = coroutine.create(function(a)
  print("got", a)                     --> got	1
  local b = coroutine.yield(a + 1)
  print("got", b)                     --> got	10
  return "done"
end)
print(coroutine.resume(co, 1))        --> true	2
print(coroutine.status(co))           --> suspended
print(coroutine.resume(co, 10))       --> true	done
print(coroutine.status(co))           --> dead
print(coroutine.resume(co))           --> false	cannot resume dead coroutine
takeaways: `resume` passes values in; `yield` passes values out, and vice versa
`coroutine.wrap` gives a function, ideal for generators
Coroutines take turns (one runs at a time) and keep their whole call stack
pitfalls: Ignoring resume's first return value: errors inside a coroutine are returned, not raised.

quiz.q: A coroutine raises an error. What does coroutine.resume return?
quiz.explain: resume works like pcall: errors come back as false plus the error object (wrap re-raises instead).

concepts.name: Garbage collection and weak tables
concepts.summary: How Lua's incremental and generational garbage collectors work, and how weak tables and __gc interact with them.
concepts.why: Long-running host programs (games, servers, editors) depend on predictable memory use and caches that don't grow forever.
concepts.body:
Lua frees memory automatically with a **garbage collector**: it periodically traces which tables, functions and strings can still be reached from your variables and frees the rest. Lua 5.4 offers two modes, switched with `collectgarbage("incremental")` or `collectgarbage("generational")`.

- **Incremental** (the library default) is a **mark-and-sweep** collector: it marks everything reachable, then sweeps away the rest, in small steps mixed in with your program so pauses stay short. The pause parameter controls how much memory grows before a new cycle starts; the step multiplier controls how much work each step does.
- **Generational** checks recently created objects often and long-lived ones rarely, which suits programs that create many short-lived tables. The standalone `lua` interpreter switches to this mode at startup.

`collectgarbage("count")` reports the memory in use (the **heap**) in kilobytes, `collectgarbage()` forces a full cycle and `"step"` does a bit of work.

A table with a metatable field `__mode` is a **weak table**: `"k"` makes keys weak, `"v"` values, `"kv"` both. A weak reference doesn't keep an object alive (normal, strong references do), so entries vanish when the object is otherwise unreachable. Use weak keys to attach data to objects you don't own and weak values for caches. Strings and numbers are values, not collectable objects, so they are never removed from weak tables. And an entry in a weak-key table is still removed even if its value refers back to its own key.

`__gc` on a table's metatable sets a **finalizer**, a function called once before the object is freed. Finalizers run in reverse order of being set, can bring the object back to life by storing it somewhere, and must be in the metatable when `setmetatable` is called. Prefer `<close>` when clean-up must happen at a known moment.
concepts.code:
local cache = setmetatable({}, {__mode = "k"})  -- weak keys

local obj = {}
cache[obj] = "metadata"
local n = 0
for _ in pairs(cache) do n = n + 1 end
print(n)                                 --> 1

obj = nil                                -- drop the only strong ref
collectgarbage()
n = 0
for _ in pairs(cache) do n = n + 1 end
print(n)                                 --> 0

local before = collectgarbage("count")
local junk = {}
for i = 1, 1e5 do junk[i] = {i} end
junk = nil
collectgarbage()
print(collectgarbage("count") < before + 100)  --> true

setmetatable({}, {__gc = function() print("finalized") end})
collectgarbage()                         --> finalized
print(collectgarbage("incremental"))     --> generational (previous mode, standalone lua)
takeaways: Two collectors: incremental (library default) and generational
`__mode = "k"`/`"v"` makes weak tables for caches and side data
`__gc` finalizers run once before collection; prefer `<close>` for timely cleanup
pitfalls: Expecting string keys in a weak-key table to disappear; strings are not collectable references.

quiz.q: You want a cache that doesn't keep its cached objects alive. Which metatable do you use?
quiz.explain: Weak values let the collector remove entries whose values are no longer referenced elsewhere.

concepts.name: Embedding Lua: the C API
concepts.summary: Build the Lua interpreter into a C program and give Lua access to C functions through Lua's virtual stack.
concepts.why: Being built into other programs is Lua's core purpose: every host program from Redis to game engines uses this C API (the set of C functions Lua offers).
concepts.body:
Lua is a library for C programs first. A host program creates an interpreter, a **Lua state**, with `luaL_newstate()`, opens the standard libraries with `luaL_openlibs`, runs code with `luaL_dostring` or `luaL_loadfile` plus `lua_pcall`, and destroys it with `lua_close`. Each `lua_State` is fully independent, so a host program can run many separate, walled-off copies of Lua.

All data passes between C and Lua through a **virtual stack**, a pile of values you add to and take from at the top. You push values (`lua_pushinteger`, `lua_pushstring`), read them by index (`lua_tointeger(L, -1)`; positive indexes count from the bottom, negative from the top) and pop them with `lua_pop`. Lua's garbage collector owns the values; while a value is on the stack it won't be freed.

A C function callable from Lua must have the form `int f(lua_State *L)`: it reads its arguments from the stack (`luaL_checkinteger(L, 1)` validates and raises a Lua error on bad input), pushes its results and returns how many it pushed. Register it with `lua_register` or, for a module, a `luaL_Reg` array and `luaL_newlib` inside a `luaopen_name` function that `require` finds via `package.cpath`.

Lua errors jump straight out of the C code with C's `longjmp`, so a C function that raises an error never returns; always run Lua code with `lua_pcall` at the top level. To keep a Lua value beyond one call, store it in the **Lua registry**, a hidden table only C code can reach (`luaL_ref`), and wrap C data in userdata with a metatable.
takeaways: All values cross between C and Lua via the virtual stack
A C function returns the number of results it pushed
Run Lua code with `lua_pcall`/`luaL_dostring`; errors jump straight out of C code
pitfalls: Leaving values on the stack in loops, which grows it until it runs out of room.

quiz.q: A C function pushes two values and returns 1. What does Lua receive?
quiz.explain: The return count tells Lua how many values from the top of the stack are results.

concepts.name: Performance and table internals
concepts.summary: How tables store array and hash parts, why locals are fast, and the habits that make Lua code quick.
concepts.why: Loops that run millions of times in games and servers need code that works with Lua's engine, not against it.
concepts.body:
Internally a table has two parts: an **array part**, a plain numbered list for integer keys 1..n, and a **hash part**, a **hash table** that finds any other key by turning it into a storage position. The array part is sized to the largest n such that more than half of the slots 1..n are in use. Outgrowing either part triggers a **rehash**, which recounts the keys and moves everything into bigger storage, so building a big table one key at a time causes several such moves; a constructor with all elements (`{a, b, c}`) sizes it once.

Lua runs your code on a **virtual machine**, a software processor with numbered slots called **registers**. **Locals live in registers** and are the fastest variables. Upvalues are close behind. Globals are lookups in the `_ENV` table (where Lua keeps them), and `math.floor` is two table lookups, which is why hot code caches them: `local floor = math.floor`.

Short strings (up to 40 bytes) are stored only once however often they appear, which is called **string interning**, and all strings are immutable. Building a string with `s = s .. x` in a loop copies the whole string so far at every step, so the work grows with the square of the length; collect the pieces in a table and call `table.concat` once.

Other habits:

- Reuse tables instead of creating new ones in inner loops, so the garbage collector has less to do.
- `#t` on a proper sequence is cheap (at worst it halves the search range repeatedly, a binary search).
- Measure with `os.clock()` before optimising; intuition is often wrong.

**LuaJIT** uses a **JIT compiler** that turns frequently run loops into machine code while the program runs, and can be many times faster, but it implements Lua 5.1 (plus some 5.2 features), so code must avoid 5.3+ features like integer subtypes and the `//` operator.
concepts.code:
local N = 200000

local t0 = os.clock()
local s = ""
for i = 1, 20000 do s = s .. "x" end      -- quadratic copying
local slow = os.clock() - t0

t0 = os.clock()
local parts = {}
for i = 1, 20000 do parts[i] = "x" end
local s2 = table.concat(parts)            -- one allocation
local fast = os.clock() - t0
print(s == s2, slow > fast)               --> true	true (usually)

local function sum_global() local x = 0
  for i = 1, N do x = x + math.sqrt(i) end return x end
local sqrt = math.sqrt
local function sum_local() local x = 0
  for i = 1, N do x = x + sqrt(i) end return x end

t0 = os.clock(); sum_global(); local g = os.clock() - t0
t0 = os.clock(); sum_local(); local l = os.clock() - t0
print(string.format("global %.4fs, local %.4fs", g, l))
takeaways: Tables have an array part and a hash part; rehash happens on growth
Locals live in registers: copy globals into locals in loops that run often
Build strings with `table.concat`, not repeated `..`
pitfalls: Optimising without measuring; use `os.clock()` or a profiler (a tool that shows where time goes) first.

quiz.q: Why is building a long string with s = s .. piece inside a loop slow?
options: Each concatenation copies the whole string so far
quiz.explain: Strings are immutable, so every step creates and copies a new, longer string, and the total work grows with the square of the length.
